editorial.summary: The Hawaii happiness inquiry continues with David Choe's mother, Jane Choe, and Critter Fleming. Jane begins with `I Am Happy` in four languages, connects family history under Japanese colonial rule to welcome rather than inherited blame, and describes late-life art made on anything available. That art becomes a test of creation without credentials: Jane works quickly and abundantly, Critter prepares seven paintings carefully, and David refuses to make either method subordinate to professional training. Airport pickup, kimchi, rice, diabetes, family travel and snorkeling lead to the episode's title-like comic line, `the turtle said yes with her eyes`; the archive keeps the joke and makes the conservation boundary explicit—wildlife cannot consent and NOAA says not to touch sea turtles. The central interview contrasts Jane's Christian happiness practice with David's attraction to chaos. Faith, apology, silence, prayer, forgiveness and `you are the masterpiece` coexist with his abandonment at age three, the LA riots, self-destructive behavior, therapy and a childhood full of hair pulling, police threats, scared-straight performances, physical fights and contradictory lessons about stealing. Mother and son openly disagree about the cornfield memory, making memory divergence part of the record rather than a problem to smooth over. The ending turns criticism and adversity into free teachers, then closes in prayer and improvised song. Every idea—including slurs, spiritual claims, body mockery, wildlife contact, self-harm language and child punishment—remains. Clinical, historical and conservation annotations sit beside the transcript instead of replacing it, private relatives and discovery trails remain protected, and no transcript turn receives a speaker name.
